newsitem.title: UK: Fashanu declines to testify to soccer bribes trial.
newsitem.headline: Fashanu declines to testify to soccer bribes trial.

text.p: Former Wimbledon striker John Fashanu will not testify at a trial in which he is charged with helping to fix soccer matches because the evidence against him is so flimsy, his lawyer said on Thursday.
Trevor Burke told the jury that Fashanu was a man of great prosperity and integrity, implying it was inconceivable he would have tried to rig games.
Defendants in English trials are under no obligation to testify or allow themselves to be cross-examined.
Burke said the only words Fashanu had uttered since being charged were "not guilty".

"Any experienced policeman or prosecutor knows those two important words convey one message to those who prosecute him -- 'Prove it if you can' -- and that is exactly what John Fashanu invites them to do," Burke said.
"You have brought him here, you prove it if you can."

Fashanu and Malaysian businessman Heng Suan Lim are charged with paying former Liverpool goalkeeper Bruce Grobbelaar and one-time Wimbledon keeper Hans Segers to rig matches on behalf of an Asian betting syndicate. All four plead not guilty.
Burke said defence witnesses would portray Fashanu as a man of great integrity.
"You will hear evidence of a personal morality that he holds which most of us cannot even begin to copy," he said. Fashanu sat impassively throughout his lawyer's speech.

In 1983 -- when Fashanu had little money and was playing for lowly Millwall -- he was offered 350,000 pounds ($574,000) to coach a predominantly white team in South Africa, then still under the apartheid regime. Fashanu rejected the offer.

"No amount of money could cause him to lose the personal sense of morality he has had. He refused on a point of principle -- that his personal integrity could not be bought even for that staggering sum of money," Burke said.
Fashanu earned a total of 2.2 million pounds from his soccer and business activities from 1990 to 1995.

The court heard that his wife Melissa Kassa-Mapsi was very wealthy in her own right, the daughter of a prominent Gabon politician who had paid 200,000 pounds in cash for a house in Gabon as a wedding present.
"Melissa is a young woman, now the mother of John's child, who is herself a woman of staggering wealth," Burke said.
The lawyer said Fashanu was a prominent figure in a large number of charities and was an unpaid ambassador to the United Nations children's charity UNICEF.
The lawyer also took a swipe at chief prosecution witness Chris Vincent, who he described as inconsistent and unreliable.
"Vincent has conceded he has never met John Fashanu, never spoken to him, never witnessed any conversation between John Fashanu and anybody else in the dock," Burke said.
"He has never seen any money passing between John Fashanu and anybody else, let alone the people in the dock."
Vincent told the court that Grobbelaar had picked up 40,000 pounds from Fashanu's London mansion in late 1993 as a reward for fixing a league match between Newcastle and Liverpool. ($1=.6097 Pound)
